title: Chapter 130 – The Fifth Log
html:
[Southern Desert – Lin Jian]

The log gives itself up one page a day, and not a line more.

He learns this on the first morning, when he sits down at the dead man's desk with a mug of Ruyan's tea and tries to read straight through. The first page lies open under the pale gold lamp, clear as print. When he turns it, the next is blank. Not faded, not stained, blank, as if the paper had never held ink. He turns it back and the first is still there. He tries the third, the tenth, the last. Nothing. The leaves lie in their stack like a deck of cards that will only be dealt one at a time.

```
DOCK — ARK-5 LOG
Access: one page per Dock-day (dawn to dawn)
Pages: 31
Note: pages are unlocked in the order they were
written. The Operator who wrote them wished
to be read slowly.
```

"He wanted to be read slowly," Yue says, when Jian shows her.

"Or he wanted to make sure I would stay thirty-one days."

"Is there a difference?"

He considers it. "Perhaps not."

So they settle in. It is not a hardship. The forbidden stair is cool and dry, and Ruyan's guards bring down bread and cold meat and jars of water twice a day, and nobody climbs down it without a long look at the ceiling. Yue sets up a corner of the room as a scriptorium, with a board across two barrels and a stack of fresh paper, and copies each page in her small fierce hand. Pebble dozes on the cot, sleeping off the Kettle. Jian reads, and thinks, and in the evenings goes up into the city and trims the temple lamps for the priests, a hundred wicks a night, in exchange for a coin and a bowl of soup. It earns him two units. Two units a night is a reasonable rate for a man who is not in a hurry.

He is, he finds, not in a hurry. It is a strange thing to discover at thirty-eight.

There is a rhythm to the days, and he comes to depend on it. Dawn: the page, read slowly, with his tea going cold. Noon: the copying, Yue's pencil scratching, the occasional argument over a word. Afternoon: sleep, in the cool, with Pebble a warm weight against his ribs. Dusk: the wicks. Night: the roof, the stars, the small cold exercise of naming the ones he still can. He keeps a tally in the margin of Yue's ledger. Five names left unspoken, so far. Five stars he can no longer find in the sky and has had to learn again from the book.

* * *

Day 3. I have made a table of what I know.

That I am in a room under a desert. That the room is cold in the morning and warm at noon. That there is a lamp which lights when I ask it and a voice in my head that says, "READY," and a pantry that I have not yet figured out how to open. That I woke with a scar and no past. That the stars outside are strange to me and also, in some way I cannot explain, entirely familiar.

That whoever left the first page was in a hurry.

I do not mean the note from E.C. at the bottom. That is the same ink as the rest, and the same hand, and I think it was written by me. I mean the paper. It is folded. It has a crease down the middle where someone shoved it into a pocket. A man who writes a letter to his successor and then folds it into quarters is not a man who has time to be neat.

Jian reads it twice.

"He is right," Yue says quietly, over her copying. "The first page is creased. Look."

He looks. A fine line runs down the center of the paper, soft with age, the ghost of a fold. He had taken it for the grain. "Why would the first Operator leave a note he had to run with?"

"Because he did not leave it." She lays down her pencil. "I think someone carried it. Seven times. From dock to dock. The same piece of paper."

"Carried by whom?"

Yue shakes her head. She is not looking at him. She is looking at the small gray beast on the cot, and the beast is looking back with her head on one side.

"Not whom," says Pebble. "What."

* * *

Day 9. I have opened the pantry.

It took me four days of feeling around the wall before I found the seam. It is behind the cot, a hairline crack running up from the floor, no wider than a thread. I put my palm to it and the voice in my head said "STEP," and I did, and was in a closet.

It is not large. Seven shelves, seven jars, each sealed with black wax and labeled in a language I cannot read but somehow understand. I did not take any of them. I do not think they are for me. I think they are for the one who comes after.

That is the oddest part of this place. Everything in it is for someone else.

Jian lays the page down.

"There is a pantry," he says.

"Behind the cot." Yue is already moving. She drags the cot aside, with Pebble clinging to the blanket, and goes down on her knees with her cheek to the wall. "Here. A crack. I can hear it. It sounds like a very small bell."

He kneels beside her. He puts his palm to the stone. And there, under his fingers, so faint that he would have missed it if Pebble had not said there, a hairline seam in the green rock, thin as a hair on a page.

The Door in his chest widens. He feels the cold flat plane of the world open under his ribs, and the seam shine out of it like a bright wire. It is no more than three paces long. He could step through it blind.

```
SEAM STEP — 4 CE (CE: 10 / 12)
```

He steps.

* * *

The pantry is a closet of green stone, perhaps four feet by six, lit by a faint glow that seems to come from the shelves themselves. The seven jars sit in a row. They are squat and heavy and wax-sealed, each as large as a man's head, and each carries a small brass tag. Yue, who has come in behind him with Pebble, bends close to read.

"Five," she says, pointing. "That one. And six. And seven." She runs her finger along the row. "The rest have no number."

"What is in them?"

"I do not know." She straightens. "But there is a paper under the fifth."

He lifts the jar. It is cold, and heavier than it looks. Beneath it lies a single slip, creased down the middle like the first page. In the cramped blue hand, fresh as dew:

Take the jar marked 5. Leave the others for the ones who come next.

It is not sufficient. It is what there is.

—E.C.

"The ones who come next," Yue repeats.

"He means the ones after me."

"Are there any?"

Jian looks at the other six jars in the green glow, their black wax glossy and unbroken. Six jars. Seven including his own. He does not answer. He lifts the fifth and cradles it in both arms, and feels, through the thick glass, a faint pulse of cold, steady heat, like a sleeping animal.

* * *

Day 17. I have been thinking about the Gate.

The voice calls it that: THE GATE. It does not say where it leads. I have asked, and it replies, "HOME." I have asked what home is. It replies, "THE PLACE YOU LEFT." I have asked where I left. It replies nothing at all.

I have started to count the days I have not wept. It is nine.

I have started to wonder why I do not remember crying.

Jian sits very still. Across the room Yue is copying, with her tongue between her teeth. The lamp burns gold and steady. In the quiet he can hear the faint dry settling of the stone around them, the old sound of a room that has been waiting for a very long time, and the slow even breath of the Dock itself, which he has begun to feel in his sleep like the pulse of an animal under his hand.

The place you left. He has heard it before, from Lan Tong, in a cold green stair. He had thought it a riddle. Now it sounds like a diagnosis.

He turns the page. And the next. And the next. A man writing alone in a room for six years, with nothing but a lamp and a cup and a voice. He sees him in these pages as in a pane of glass: a tired, stubborn, deliberate man, a materials scientist, from the careful way he describes the stone, who takes inventory of everything and complains of nothing. He is funny, sometimes. He draws a cartoon of the voice in his head as a small officious clerk with spectacles. He invents a game with the cup. He sings.

He is lonely. He does not say so. He only writes, on the eleventh day of the fourth month: I found myself telling the lamp a joke. It did not laugh. I told it again.

Jian puts his hand over his mouth and does not move for a long while.

* * *

The high priest of the lamps is a stooped old woman named Zhen, with cataracts like pearls and hands as steady as a surgeon's, and on the nineteenth evening she catches Jian's sleeve as he is trimming a wick on the eastern terrace.

"You are the one who goes down," she says.

"Yes."

"I knew it the first night." She smiles, showing three teeth. "The lamps lean toward you. A hundred thousand little flames, all pointing to one man. I thought the god had sent someone at last."

"I am not a god."

"No. Gods are tidy." She runs a thumb along the clay niche. "My grandmother told me the story of the sleeping lamp. Not the pilgrim story. The true one. She said that it was never a lamp. It was a room, with a man in it, who lit a flame every night so that anyone passing would know there was someone home. He did it for six years. And then one night, a woman in a veil came and spoke to him at the top of the stair, and he put the flame out, and went away."

"Went where?"

"She did not know. She only knew that the people loved him. They had not known he was there, you see, until the light went out, and then they missed it." Zhen turns her pearl-white eyes on him. "So they lit a thousand lamps, in his memory. And then ten thousand. And then they forgot why."

Jian has stopped trimming. The wick smolders between his fingers.

"Do you know his name?"

"I know that it was short." The old woman laughs, a dry rattle. "I know that they called him the Lamplighter. The one who keeps a light for strangers." She pats his hand. "You have the same look about you. The look of someone who sits in a room alone and calls it duty. I hope you do it better than he did."

"How did he do it?"

"Badly," says Zhen cheerfully. "He told jokes to the flame."

She pats him again, and shuffles off along the terrace, and does not look back. Behind her, a hundred thousand wicks lean after her in the dusk. He stands alone with his trimming-knife in the wind, and discovers that his eyes are wet.

Day 21. A woman came to the stair today.

She wore a veil of plum-colored gauze and carried a book under her arm, a heavy thing with a cloth cover. She stopped at the top of the forbidden stair and did not come down. She said, in a dry voice, that she was the Keeper of the Roll, and that she had come to see whether the Operator was well.

I said I was well. I said I was lonely. She did not seem to find this strange.

She told me that there was an Order, that it had been founded to serve me, and that its purpose was a kindness. She said that when I was ready, I would be offered a way home. She said it with great care, the way one speaks to a man holding a knife.

I asked, "What happens to the Operators who go?"

She said, "They are restored."

I asked, "To what?"

She did not answer. After a while she bowed and went up the stair. I have not seen her since. I think she was sad. I think she was ashamed.

I have written down what she said, word for word, because it seems to me that when I go through the Gate, I will not remember it. I would like to be able to forgive her.

Jian puts down the page. His hand is not quite steady.

"A Keeper," Yue whispers. "Six hundred years ago."

"The Order's third Keeper. The first to meet an Operator." He looks at the tiny veiled shape that his mind builds from the words. "Sang Ruo would have known her name."

"Would she have told you?"

"She would have told me it was in the Roll." He gives a small, bitter laugh. "And that she could not read it."

Pebble, on the cot, lifts her head. "She was ashamed," she says. "That is what a seam sounds like. Where the shame is. A person who is ashamed has a gap where the thing they did used to be." She yawns. "I know a great many ashamed people. They are all very polite."

* * *

Ruyan visits on the twenty-sixth night, in the small hours, with a lantern and a bottle of plum wine and a face that has been awake too long.

She does not come down. She sits on the third step of the forbidden stair, with her sword across her knees and her back to the dark, and calls through the open door for him to come out to her. He does. They sit side by side on the cold stone, not speaking, and she pours two cups.

"I have news," she says. "I did not want to tell it before the sister."

"What news?"

"Registry runners." She sips. "Six, in the last month. Not sent by the House. They carry plum-colored passes that are two years out of date and they wear no seals. They come into the city one at a time, in rags, and they ask the lamp-sellers whether a young man with a scar on his left hand has passed through." She turns the cup in her hand. "They ask very politely. Then they sit down in the road and wait."

"The Unkept."

"Is that what you call them?" She does not seem surprised. "My priests call them hollow men. They do not eat, as far as I can tell. They do not drink. They do not sleep. They sit at the Pilgrims' Gate and watch the road, and when the caravans go out they follow, at a distance, like dogs."

"How many?"

"Eleven, as of tonight."

Jian says nothing.

"I do not like it, Lin Jian." Her voice is low. "I am a practical woman. I do not believe in curses. But I have thirty years of ledger-keeping behind me and I know what it looks like when a debt is coming due. Whatever you did in the north, whatever the House is, it has noticed that you are in the south." She drains her cup. "And it has a great many patient men."

"I will leave in the morning."

"No." She stands, brushing off her robe. "You will leave when the log is finished, as you must. And in the meantime I will keep the gate. But I want a promise."

"What promise?"

"When you come back through Sunken Lamp, if you come back, you will tell me what the lamp was." Her smile is brief and crooked. "I have spent my life selling cloth to people who wanted to be forgotten. I would like, just once, to know what I am sitting on."

"I will tell you."

"Good." She turns to go. "Drink the wine. It is a very bad vintage, and it will make you feel better about your life."

He drinks it. It does.

The letter from home comes on the twenty-fourth day, in a bamboo tube, carried by a Tan courier who has ridden three weeks on a changing relay of horses.

He opens it on the forbidden stair, in the cool, with the lamps of Sunken Lamp winking above him. It is in Wenyuan's laborious hand, with Qinghe's neat corrections in the margin, and a drawing from Feng's youngest, a girl of four, of a stick figure standing beside a larger stick figure holding a spoon.

Dear son,

We are well. Your mother says to tell you that you are not to worry, and then to tell you everything, so I will. The Seat has been recognized in the Hall of Elders. Feng sits in your sister's chair when she is gone, and has not made a single speech. The harvest was good. Hu has made a second tool-arm and is teaching it to dance. Bai is slower but cheerful. The roots have gone to the ninth, every season, and each time the boy comes back, he says she is still breathing.

Your cousin Hui writes from the Sect that he is Core-bound and you are not to ask what that means.

My hands are cold. Your mother has sewn me a pair of lined gloves and I look very foolish. I have not complained once. She says I complain constantly, but she is mistaken.

The clan is four hundred and fifty-one. We lost old Dull Gu in the autumn. He went in his sleep. He was ninety-one and he had said eight words that week. We buried him on the hill he wanted, and the whole Garden came. I thought you would want to know.

Write when you can. Send Yue home when it is time. I know she will argue.

Your father,

Wenyuan

(Your mother says: eat properly.)

He reads it three times. Then he folds it carefully and puts it in the breast of his robe, beside the spoon.

* * *

Yue does argue.

It happens on the thirty-first day, at the desk, with the last page lying open on its stone under the lamp. They have both read it. The final entry of Operator Five is short, written in a hand that has grown shaky, dated the last day of the sixth year.

I am going to the Gate. I have been given a choice, and I have chosen. The voice asked me, "HOME?" and I said yes.

I do not know what will happen. I think I will wake up somewhere else. I think I may not remember this. I am writing it down so that if I do remember, I will know that I was right; and if I do not, I will know that I was brave.

If the one who reads this is me, I am sorry.

—E.C. (fifth)

There is nothing after. The remaining pages, as the Dock announced, are blank.

"He went through," says Yue, very softly. "Like the others."

"Yes."

"And woke somewhere else."

"Presumably."

"Then the loop is real." She turns to him, and her face in the gold light is very white. "He did not die. He left. He wrote to himself so that he could be brave. And then he was forgotten, and sent again."

"I do not know that."

"You do." She says it with terrible simplicity. "You knew when you saw the creased paper. You knew when you read the note. You are only waiting for someone else to say it aloud."

He does not answer. In the silence, Pebble climbs onto the desk and sits between them with her paws together, looking from one face to the other.

"I am going home," says Yue.

It is not what he expected. She says it without drama, with her chin up and her hands folded on the ledger. "I said six months. It has been eight. Father is waiting. The Seat is waiting. And you are going west, and I cannot go west." She swallows. "I am not a coward. I will go with you, if you ask. But I think you will not."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I will not know what is waiting at the next one," he says. "And I will not know if I can bring you back." He hears his own voice shake. "I have a family I cannot afford to lose. You are the family."

"I know." She smiles, crookedly, and wipes her eyes with the heel of her hand. "That is why I am going. You need someone to be home."

* * *

They leave her at the Pilgrims' Gate on the morning of the thirty-second day, in a cold wind and a gray dawn.

The Tan caravan is ready: eight wagons, forty guards, Tan Bo on the lead box with his hat pulled low. Ruyan has chosen the route herself, the long way round through the oases, with a score of her own men to ride beside the wagon that carries Yue's pack. She does not speak. She stands with her arms folded and a face like shut stone.

Yue embraces her. Then Ruyan, to Jian's astonishment, embraces her back.

"Keep the ledger," Ruyan says gruffly. "I want it copied. All of it."

"I have copied it twice."

"Make it three." She lets go. "Go home, Lin Yue. Hold the door."

Yue turns. She comes to Jian last, and takes both his hands in hers, and holds them hard. She is small and thin and her eyes are the color of dark tea. She does not cry, and he is grateful.

"I will hear you," she says.

"Hear me?"

"From home. Pebble has a bell." She reaches into her pack and draws out a small round silver bell, no bigger than a plum stone, strung on a red thread. "It is from the Garden. It rang once in the well, the year I turned eleven, when the door in the cellar stuck. It has a seam in it. Pebble will wear it. If you are ever in trouble, she can ring it." She ties the thread round the little beast's neck with trembling fingers. "I will hear it. Whatever the distance. I will hear it in the Garden, in my sleep, in my bones."

"You cannot know that."

"I cannot," she agrees. "I am going to anyway."

Pebble stands very still while the thread is tied. Then she lifts her head and presses her small gray face against Yue's palm.

"You will not need it," she says clearly. "But I will keep it."

Yue's mouth shakes. "Take care of him."

"Always," says Pebble.

They watch the wagons go out through the Pilgrims' Gate and down the long white road toward the dunes, eight dim shapes in the dust, growing smaller. Yue sits at the back of the last one with her ledger on her knees. She does not wave. She only keeps looking back, and Jian keeps looking forward, until the dust takes her, and there is only a smudge on the sky, and a bell on a red thread, and a long cold wind coming up from the west.

He stands there until it is gone. Then he shoulders his pack, lifts the heavy jar into his arms, and turns toward the setting stars.

The Nameless is waiting at the gate.

It falls in, forty paces behind, without a word.
